extra.message: A SQL statement is built by inserting values into a string. If any of those values can come from a visitor (URL, form, header, cookie), they can rewrite the query and read or delete other customers' data (SQL injection). Use parameters (?, impo) or the ORM's safe query builder. Verify whether the inserted value can be influenced by a user.

Any website may call this API from a visitor's browser. That's fine for public data; it's a problem for anything that relies on cookies or returns personal data. List the allowed origins instead.

JSON.parse runs inside a stream callback without try/catch. One request with a malformed body throws an uncaught exception, which crashes the whole Node.js process and takes the site down for everyone. Wrap it in try/catch and answer 400. Also cap the body size.

A token is decoded without checking its signature. If this decides who the user is, anyone can forge a token and log in as anyone. Use a signed token and verify it (jwt.verify, your auth provider's SDK, or an HMAC check with a server-side secret). Decoding without verifying is only OK for display purposes in the browser.

This outgoing HTTP call has no timeout. If the other service (payment, email, shipping API...) slows down during your peak, every request waits forever, and your server runs out of capacity even though your own code is fine. Add signal: AbortSignal.timeout(3000) (or similar) and handle the failure.

Blocking (synchronous) work inside a request handler. Node.js serves every visitor on one thread, so while this runs nobody else gets served. Read static files once at startup (or serve them from a CDN) and use the async versions of these calls.

A database call runs once per item in a loop (the "N+1 query" problem). A page with 50 items makes 51 round-trips to the database. At normal traffic it's unnoticeable; at flash-sale traffic it's often the first thing to melt. Fetch everything in one query (JOIN / WHERE id IN (...) / ORM include/eager loading).

A SQL statement is built by inserting values into a string. If any of those values can come from a visitor (URL, form, header, cookie), they can rewrite the query and read or delete other customers' data (SQL injection). Use parameters (?, imp) or the ORM's safe query builder. Verify whether the inserted value can be influenced by a user.

The request carries "price". Check what the server does with it: prices, totals and discounts must come from your database, never from the browser, or buyers can pay whatever they like by editing the request.

The new stock/balance value is calculated in application code and written back ("SET stock = ?"). When two shoppers buy at the same moment, both read the same number and one purchase overwrites the other (lost update), so you can sell more than you have. Do the arithmetic in one atomic statement instead: UPDATE ... SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = ? AND stock > 0, and check that one row changed.

The visitor waits while an email/SMS is sent. That adds hundreds of milliseconds to every order and fails the order if the email provider is slow. Put the message on a background queue and respond immediately.
Privileged-looking route. Confirm it (1) requires authentication, (2) checks the caller is an admin, and (3) is disabled in production if it's a test/debug/seed route.

Error details (stack trace) are sent to the visitor. They reveal file paths, library versions and sometimes data, which helps attackers. Log the details server-side and return a generic message with a request id.
